utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. And good morning to everybody in New York. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Carmela Javier, Lorna Bolton, Evangelos Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Kate Marshall, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Sacirbey, again, let's go through the ritual, still bound which the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, it's understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Sacirbey. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We had left off yesterday discussing whether or not you had formally made mention of your criticism of Mr. Akashi and General Rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can we have 1D03-0796 up on the screen, which would be tab number 43.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I have that, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a letter, if I'm not mistaken, it was written on the 25th of October, 1994. Its distribution is general. And by that I understand that this is a letter that was distributed to the General Assembly and to the Security Council; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And turning to the letter itself, if we could, as I understand this letter --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I understand this letter, this is a letter that came from representative parliamentary parties of the assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which you forwarded in your capacity as the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 2 of the letter itself. In paragraph 2 the letter states: "In this respect, the conduct of Lieutenant-General Sir Michael Rose commander of the United Nations protected force [UNPROFOR) in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in diverting the attention and resolve of the free world from punishing criminal acts and fascism to peripheral issues is unacceptable." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is a position that you adopted in your capacity as ambassador; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this letter is forwarded by the leadership of, I believe, if not all most of the political parties in the parliament at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked to adopt it; I was only asked to pass it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this point I'm saying in your capacity as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, you adopted the assertions made in this letter, did you not? This is not something that you were trying to shy away from, is it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me, did I personally agree and did I espouse some of these views at the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But in order to forward this letter, I did not have to agree or disagree with the assertions made therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's understood. Going to the last paragraph of the first page it says: "We therefore request that the Lieutenant-General Sir Michael Rose relinquish his current post and duties. We request an objective and impartial commander who would carry out the implementation of United Nations resolutions on the ground, an individual," next page, please, "who would serve legitimate United Nations interests, rather than the interests of his/her national government." And then it's signed by, as I understand it, a number of representative parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you share the opinion and did you espouse the opinion in your capacity as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina that Lieutenant-General Sir Michael Rose was involved in operating for the interests of his national government as opposed to -- [overlapping speakers]... the interests of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that sense you mean the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I believe -- I believe General Rose can be characterised in terms of his behaviour in many ways. One of them is potentially that at times he gave greater due consideration to the interest of his national government than, let's say, the United Nations. But I do not believe that that was in fact the particular issue that was at stake here or the one that was really being addressed, as I think I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm just trying to understand the language here, which is the language at the end of the paragraph says: "... an individual who would serve legitimate United Nations interests rather than the interest of his/her national government." That seems to be relatively focused language, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It sure does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you asked me did I share this view personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. No, I asked you whether you shared the view in your capacity as ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said I don't have to share the view in order --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is not my question, Mr. Sacirbey. Mr. Sacirbey, my question is not whether you have to or do not have it; that I appreciate. My question is, Did you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As best to some degree but really not to the degree stated in this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, can I have this marked as Defendant's next in order. Can we please have on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be given Exhibit D152. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Next could we have 1D03-4599. Mr. Registrar, that will be document number 12 in the first packet that was provided to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just to make sure that we are on the same page, I trust you are looking at "New York Times" article dated November 5 1994, entitled arms trafficking to Bosnia goes on despite embargo, by Roger Cohen.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, once again this is a periodical that I believe you are familiar with, the "New York Times."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to this specific article concerning the trafficking of arms to Bosnia on November of 1994, is this an article that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph number 1 it states: "... Even as United Nations discusses lifting the arms embargo on Bosnia and Herzegovina, the embargo appears to have become largely a fiction openly flouted." Right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the matter of discussing lifting the arms embargo, one of your primary focuses as the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina was to get the embargo lifted, was it not? I understand you had many others?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to November of 1994, at this point I take it that you were obtaining some traction in your diplomatic efforts in regards to being able to openly obtain weapons of war. You were beginning to get a shift in the tide.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me for two minutes, Mr. Sacirbey, I'm having a slight technical problem, but I'll be okay in a minute, I think. We're fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to, for a moment, if I could, perhaps, discuss your function as a diplomat, and specifically as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the particular issue of weapons and war. And I'd like to ask you to comment on the following, if you could: "Diplomacy is often popularly thought of as the peaceful alternative to violence, but in fact, diplomacy serves to prepare as often as to avoid war. It is an important part of waging war. It often makes the difference in who wins and nearly always codifies war's results. Again, diplomacy is the verbal representation of compelling international realities, and military force is one of those realities." Would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in all, but in part. I certainly was not in Bosnian diplomacy when the war started out, so to talk of preparation for war was beyond my experience. But I certainly did find that in fact diplomacy did legitimize, codify as you've used the word, the consequences of war, and in my opinion at times the consequences of genocide. And I think that was one of unfortunate results of what we have come to call diplomacy and the Dayton Accords in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go back to the article that we were looking at. And if we could go to page 2 of the article, which is discussing the effects of increase in arms. It says: "The effect of this increase in arms available to the Bosnian Muslim and allied Bosnian Croat forces has been evident in the last week in two successful offensives against the long-dominant Bosnian Serbs. The first offensive burst through Serbian lines east of Bihac in the north-west; the second resulted in the capture of the town of Kupres in the west central part of the country." Now, with regard to those particular battles, those are battles that you were aware of, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to battles in general, going to the summer of 1994, there was a relatively strong offensive in June, was there not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in June of what year? I didn't hear you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of an offensive in June 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Moving to the next page, I'm not sure it's the same in terms of e-court, but it would be the bottom paragraph on page 3 where it says: "Apart from east Europe, the other major source of arms in trafficking valued at about $500 million in the last two years appears to have been Muslim countries. Mr. Beaver and other analysts estimated that Iran alone had provided at least 1500 tons of ammunition that reached Bosnia through Croatia." Is that figure there, the figure of 1500 tons of ammunition, a figure that you were aware of whilst you were --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just don't have personal knowledge of these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any reason to dispute these numbers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I have no knowledge one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, sorry. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In my view it's not an appropriate question, and he doesn't have reason to dispute it. He either knows it or he doesn't know it. He said he doesn't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He said he doesn't have personal knowledge. If he has other kinds of knowledge, then he may have a reason to dispute it, he may not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any other kinds of reasons to know about these figures, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Not beyond what I've really seen in general media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's just be clear about this, apart from your general media reports, did you not receive what we've termed on-the-ground information concerning what assets your army actually had?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only reports I would receive is what was necessary for defence, particularly anti-tank weapons. The value of such assets, the amount of such assets, and where they may have been designated is not something that was linked to my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with regard to the value of such assets, you've told us that you had some meetings at least with some Russian delegates in which there was a discussion about the purchase of various armaments. Now, my question to you is, Did you discuss a price, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, could I have a page references for that discussion from my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're looking at looking at the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, just hold on. We are looking at a page on the screen, Madam, which -- whose last paragraph starts with "apart from East Europe."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, but was there a specific reference to some meetings at -- with Russian delegates, which there was a discussion of the purchase of various armaments?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, and I think Mr. Sacirbey confirmed this yesterday in passing and we will get to it, you had meetings with delegates from --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. You had meetings from delegates who were from Russia, and there was a discussion about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith, you can't ignore your learned friend who is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. Your learned friend doesn't understand how you link those meetings with this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The way that I link the meetings with the paragraph is because, as you said, it's eastern Europe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What I'm asking my friend to do, Your Honour, is -- in accordance with the guide-lines, is that not to para-phrase what a witness has said, but to actually put to them what they said previously when called been to do so. So this is just part of the evidence from yesterday that I don't recall if it was from yesterday, and I'm simply asking my friend to tell me where it appears in the transcript so I can be sure he is being accurate in his wording of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fair enough, and we'll -- we will attend to that. Now, I'll move on for a second until we pull up the specific page reference here. I move the admission of this particular document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit D153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During your time as an ambassador, you were concerned about the fact that UNPROFOR was delivering fuel to Bosnian Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I don't recall the specifics of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it refresh your recollection if I were to include in your concern that you had been told that the reason that UNPROFOR was delivering such fuel was to engage in clearing the roads of snow. And you had taken the position that this is an "example of how UNPROFOR's resources are pruned to serve the interests of a war machine."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whose war machine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I think I remember the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. That would be the Serbian war machine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, again, did not hear you on that last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would have been, as you put it, the Serbian war machine, because His Honour asked which war machine.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from -- this is something that you actually raised in front of the Security Council, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a point I haven't, frankly, revisited for many years so I'm trying to recollect. I believe I did, but I just, again, I have not had the opportunity to refresh my memory for a long time on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have 1D03-0648, tab 34, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if you have that yet, sir. Oh, you do, good.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I believe. We are talking about a 9 November 1994 Security Council --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct. If you look at the second column it says: "Today I was informed that the Serbians will in fact be given more fuel by UNPROFOR, in order, ostensibly, to clear the roads of snow. This is but one example of how UNPROFOR's resources are pruned to serve the interests of a war machine." Does that --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection with regard to your complaint in this regard -- by that I mean that UNPROFOR was supplying fuel to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, not being particularly fresh on the circumstances here, but these are obviously my words and I -- my memory is adequately refreshed, at least as to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the first page of this document. I see this first page talks of a letter dated 3rd November, 1994, from the permanent representative from Pakistan to the United Nations addressed to the president of the Security Council. Is that what is contained, what you are referring to or -- I'm trying to see whether what was being quoted --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey made a speech at that time, and I'm using this solely for the purposes of refreshing his recollection. I don't intend on introducing this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that part of his speech that you quoted to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... Thank you. You may proceed. You are not tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm not. If we could now have 1D03-4607, which would be tab 14 in the original group of articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's an article entitled "US looks away as Iran arms Bosnia." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 1, it states: "'The Clinton Administration has chosen to ignore weapons shipments from Iran to the Muslim-led Bosnian government that in the last year have added considerably to Bosnian's military fire-power,' American officials said today. 'They said that the United States has ample evidence of the Iranian deliveries, which are in violation of the United Nations embargo that bans arms shipments to all combatants in the Bosnian civil war, but they said the Administration had not tried in any way to cut off the flow. The Administration said last fall that it would no longer take part in efforts to enforce the embargo on shipments to the Bosnians.'" Now, you told us yesterday that you had a conversation with Mr. Holbrooke, my question to you is, was the conversation that you had with Mr. Holbrooke in the fall of 1994 with regard to this particular matter, which is that there would not be any enforcement of the embargo by the United States, but there also would be, if I understood your testimony correctly, willing to assist in this regard, in getting you arms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the last part of your question, but I am very clear that we were told by Ambassador Holbrooke that in exchange for not pressing or the lifting of the arms embargo in the US Congress. In fact, weapons would be allowed to flow from any source, and again citing his words exactly, including Iran. Whether that meant the United States itself would directly participate, if that's what your question is, I'm not sure I'm in a position to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you are not in a position to respond to that, are you asserting any kind of privilege, or are you saying that you don't know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have personal knowledge directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you don't have personal knowledge directly, I take it what you are telling us is that you did not hear from the horse's mouth, in this sense, Ambassador Holbrooke, that the United States would be actively assisting in supplying you with weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Had you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Had you obtained such information from other sources?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again wishing to be entirely clear on this point, there were reasons to believe that in fact there were other -- there was other assistance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, your attempt to be clear has left me somewhat confused, so I need to pursue this a bit. You say there was reason to believe that in fact there was other assistance. Could you kindly explain to the Chamber what you mean by that statement, that there was reason to believe that in fact there was other assistance.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe you are aware, by 1995 there were various types of military institutions, private or quasi-private that were engaged in providing training and assistance, particularly in Croatia. Whether that included anything more tangible beyond strategic assistance, I'm not sure, nor would I have any reason to have been directly privy to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to what you've just said, you said there were various types of military institutions, private or quasi-private. I'm not sure that I am understanding what you are saying here. And perhaps, once again, you can be of some assistance to the Chamber in this regard. When you're talking about military institutions, are you referring to military institutions of states, or are you referring to some kind of military institution, for example, a private institution such as Blackwater?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of such institutions may have been very different than Blackwater which served mainly, as I understand it, in the Iraq war, had serves as a form of private contract that's providing security. The institutions that I'm familiar with would have had to have received approval from the US government, the Pentagon, and the State Department, but in fact were not, at least as far as I am aware of, an institution of the US government, but in fact operated as private corporations. So the comparison to Backwater is only somewhat appropriate here in the sense that they were in fact private enterprises, as I understand them. To what extent they were linked to governments, I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicate in your last answer: "The institutions I'm familiar with would have had to receive approval from the US government, the Pentagon, and the State Department." So with regard to the institutions that you are familiar with, could you please identify for the Chamber those institutions that you are familiar with, that you state would have to have received approval from the US government, the Pentagon, or the State Department?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To give you the context of how I'm familiar with these institutions, at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am sorry, I'm asking you for you to -- I'm asking for you to answer the question now, as opposed to jump around it. And I'm asking you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To identify the institutions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must, again, emphasise that I would need to have my memory refreshed as to the actual name, but my opinion is that these institutions were cited even in the media, so I'm sure would not be very difficult to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm not in a position here to refresh your memory, and I'm really following --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- your lead here, because this is something that you have brought up to us.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which is that there were some private institutions, from what I understand your answer, had some form of government sanction that you were aware of.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And could you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the names, I'm sorry, I just don't recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who did you have -- did you have conversations with any of your colleagues at the United Nations concerning this matter, and by colleagues, I'm not talking about your own delegation, but other diplomats of other member states?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other than Croatia, probably not. And the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. If we could go back to the article, I believe we were on page -- I think it's on page 2. And going down to the -- the paragraph that starts with "Mr. Clinton": It says: "Mr. Clinton had said it would be unwise for the United States to flout the United Nations resolution. But today his top aides noted carefully that nothing in the resolution requires the United States to report violations." Now, with regard to the issue of 713 and the reporting of violations, was the topic a matter of common conversation either formally or informally at the United Nations, that there was no necessity to report violations of the embargo by member states?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the US government you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, by member states.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the United States?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, by member states.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the context of one state here, United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So with regard to the balance of the member states, there was no discussion as to whether or not any other member states would have a duty under 713 to report violations of the embargo.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were such discussions. No, there were such discussions involving other states as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, and with regard to the discussions involving other states, be they informal or formal, am I accurate in my assumption that it was incumbent upon member states to inform the United Nations, General Assembly, or Security Council, or -- of violations of the embargo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not believe such an international legal obligation existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Was it a matter that was discussed as being an important component part independent of whether or not it was deemed to be a legal obligation in terms of making sure there was not a flow of arms and weapons? By that I'm referring to a reporting requirement.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... As a practical consideration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could go to the last paragraph in that document. It states: "After congress," that's, I'm assuming, the United States Congress -- "passed legislation that would have cut off all money for enforcing the embargo by November 15th, the Administration directed the United States military to stop enforcing the prohibition." Now, is this something that you were made aware of in your capacity as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that money had been cut off from forcing --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. There are two parts here, one is that money was cut off for enforcing the embargo. And the other part is that the United States Administration had directed the military to stop enforcing the embargo. You were aware of both of those things; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "Even that step angered Britain, France, other countries whose farces are among the United Nations peacekeepers in Bosnia and who have warned that any new flow of arms to either side in the war will only make future battles more violent." Now, were you privy to at the United Nations, either in the hallways informally or formally at the General Assembly or the Security Council, this aspect of the debate, which is that the United States had made a determination that it was no longer going to, at least surreptitiously, support the flow of arms into your country, but rather was going to openly take the position that it was not going to enforce the embargo, and Britain and France, among other member states, were of a different mind?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the debate ranged from the paragraph that you just read to the last paragraph in this article, which stresses, of course, the still vast imbalance in the military weight of, if you would, the combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think in that context, that was a constant point of debate and discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have that marked as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit D154. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have 1D0 -- 1D00-4539 up on the screen, which would be tab 93, Mr. Registrar, in your new binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if you had a chance to -- to look at the document. Good. I'd like to, after you've had a chance to take a look at the first page, and for purposes of --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is an UNPROFOR -- of 2 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And for purposes of clarification, so that the Chamber is aware, a certain part of this document is already in evidence as Defendant's 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do is take a look at page 1, if you would initially, and going to -- I apologise, Mr. Registrar. And looking at the -- go down to the 1, 2, 3, the fourth bullet point, it says: "UNPROFOR relations with the Bosnian government are deteriorating; freedom of movement is restricted." Were you made aware by your president or your military that the Bosnian army, and by that I mean the BiH Army was restricting the freedom of movement of UNPROFOR during this time.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in fact, I was present on several situations where UNPROFOR and the Bosnian government and military had to share the same roads. The roads that were to be secured through Serbian control areas in fact were no longer made available to UNPROFOR. So UNPROFOR in fact would use the road, the only connection that the Bosnian government maintained, which was over Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to page 4, please, which discusses this particular bullet point. If we could go to the section that starts off -- it's in the bottom part of the page, Mr. Registrar. It says: "UNPROFOR relations" --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If we could scroll down. It says: "UNPROFOR relations with the Bosnian government deteriorating. UNPROFOR's relations with the Bosnian government seems to be getting worse. The Bosnians claim that UNPROFOR is doing nothing to help Bosnia or to implement its mandate; that UNPROFOR is trying to ensure that the Reserve Force is ineffectual; and that UNPROFOR is doing nothing to retrieve the large amount of (principally French) military equipment still held by the Serbs, and being used by the Serbs to attack the Bosnians. The situation seems to have got worse following a number of statements from senior Bosnian politicians." The first one being on Monday June 26th. Attributed to Prime Minister Silajdzic, stating: "The United Nations organisation is an accomplice in this genocide against Bosnia and its people, because it does not protect Bosnia." The next on the 27th of June, Foreign Minister Sacirbegovic, which I believe is you, sir, stated that:

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: UNPROFOR's presence is no longer in the interests of Bosnia's civilians or government, but the interests of certain western powers. We do have a choice, which is clearly to tell the international community that we no longer consent to the presence of UNPROFOR in our country. Is that a statement that you made, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is that a statement that you made with relation to -- I'm using the term broadly for the moment -- with relation to your displeasure in the manner in which UNPROFOR was following its mandate?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at this point in time we are not talking about pleasure, approval or disapproval, as much as we are talking about the fact that UNPROFOR was in effect powerless to address its most -- the most important elements of its mandate. In fact was sharing resources with the Bosnian government, everything from roads to even things like food and medicine. And obviously at that point in time had become in effect a third consideration in the conflict. What I mean by that is that when issues were to be considered in terms of more effective measures to bring about an end to the conflict or to confront those who might be besieging Sarajevo or other enclaves, the safety of UNPROFOR personnel was always a primary concern and one to which frequently the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina and of course the country itself became secondary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: So in this sense --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. So let me ask you a question based upon what you've just said --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My friend cut off the witness. He was answering the question responsively, I think, and he hadn't finished. And I think he ought to be given the opportunity to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do want to finish up, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour. Just to be very brief, I think the point was, is that the UN forces, themselves, had in fact become threatened. And in defending themselves, particularly against the Serbian forces, it was the considerations of their security that sometimes took primacy over their mandate in defending the civilian population or even providing adequate humanitarian assistance to the civilian population. So in this way, when we addressed what means might be necessary to bring about peace, to bring about an end to the conflict, too frequently the issue was, Well, what are the consequences for the UN personnel on the ground? Would there in fact be reprisals, and should those reprisals be considered in setting forth strategy in the implementation of UN mandates?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Mr. Sacirbey. Please do correct me if I'm wrong; with regard to the first person who died in Srebrenica, that was an UNPROFOR soldier who was killed by a member of the BiH Army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that in fact a Dutch soldier was killed, and it seems that it was a Bosnian army or a Bosnian individual. But in fact, as I understand it, the investigation was never concluded, since Srebrenica fell before such investigation could be concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. As a matter of fact, you know it was the BiH army, and you engaged in diplomatic intervention with the Dutch foreign ministry and the Dutch Department of Defence over this particular issue, including attending the funeral of this young soldier; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend the funeral unfortunately, and I would have. I would like to pay respect to all those who came to Bosnia whatever the results of their actions may have been. But nonetheless, I did in fact certainly engage with the Dutch government and did provide my condolences. And did in fact even provide whatever consideration may have been appropriate at the time in view of the possibility that such Dutch soldier may have been killed by those defenders of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to a question I'd asked you earlier, you had indicated that you were not aware of a June offensive in 1994. You most assuredly are aware of a June offensive in 1995, are you not? And by a June offensive I mean a June offensive by the Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. If you would like to be more specific around which town, and I believe you are speaking of Sarajevo here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm starting with --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly an effort to -- the siege of Sarajevo, and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to Sarajevo, at that time it was a fact, was it not, that the Bosnian army placed their mortars wherever they wanted, including close to the Kosevo hospital and the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I'm unaware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Were you aware of the view that had been espoused by some individuals in UNPROFOR that a gentleman by the name of Muratovic -- do you know who he is? Morotovic or Muratovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are speaking of Mr. Hasan Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you identify him, please. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was the minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina responsible for United Nations affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is dealing with the UN forces on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was a concern at that time, that this gentleman and the Bosnia-Herzegovina army were attempting to force UNPROFOR into a situation where the daily use of the road from Mount Igman would provoke a Bosnian Serb response?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such an effort, no. In fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was that a --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were quite troubled by the fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you are not aware of it, you are not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer, or would you -- no, but I -- you are speaking of the Mount Igman road, and it did provide us with some real issues because in fact the road was constantly under used during the evening which is considered the safest time to travel. And in fact the UN forces then only felt safe to travel at night. And clearly there were numerous times when the road in fact was not useable by all the traffic that in fact wanted to use it, including Bosnian, military, and/or government traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that the UN forces then only felt safe to travel at night, as a matter of fact there were a variety of agreements that were put forth with regard to the use of that particular road. And by virtue of the fact we received this information in closed session, I'm going to ask you whether or not you are aware of the fact there being an agreement between members of UNPROFOR and the BiH army with regard to the use of this road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm having trouble understanding, I think, the key word in your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The key word being agreement.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was -- can you just repeat the question. [Overlapping speakers] ... sometimes you say in the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I mention --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. The interpreters are unable to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... can't go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters are complaining. They are saying you are overlapping, and they can't follow you, number one. Number two, maybe it might help at this stage just to ask -- at this stage perhaps it might be helpful just to caution both counsel and witness to be brief in both their questions and answers. It's very difficult to follow what you gentlemen are talking about, and there is quite often a straying off either from the question or from the answer. If you could ask very pointed questions and give very pointed answers, we might perhaps make better progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you aware of there being an agreement between UNPROFOR and the BiH army for the use of Mount Igman road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of some agreement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Returning to the document that we were referring to before. Continuing: "In a letter to the Security Council dated Wednesday, 28 June, he implied that consent might be withdrawn if UNPROFOR and the reserve force, did not become more" -- and I'm sorry, I can't read the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: More vigorous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "... vigorous in the Prosecution of the UN mandate." Is that a position that you took?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a fair view.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And on the 29th of June, the gentleman who you previously identified, Mr. Muratovic stated: "The Bosnian government wanted," and it says, "more dealings with SRSG Akashi, 'who is dead for us.'" I take it that there is a word missing here. It should be "no more dealings." If we could go back a page.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can actually see that word in my draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, very good. Excellent. And on Friday the 30th of June, going back to the next page: "... the mayor of Sarajevo hinted at retaliation against UNPROFOR if it did nothing to help the city." Is this something that you were aware of, that the mayor of Sarajevo had said that there was going to be retaliation against UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It goes on to say UNPROFOR's freedom of movement is blocked. Not so much in the city itself, as on the routes in Sector South west that lead to Igman road. This has the effect of delaying convoys over Mount Igman by up to a day, and sometimes more. Inside the city, UNPROFOR no longer has access to hospitals, or to other locations of special interest." In your capacity as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, whilst you were at the United Nations, were you made aware of the fact that UNPROFOR's access had been restricted and blocked as mentioned in this telex?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in fact I was foreign minister at the time. And second of all, as you can see by the letter, it doesn't speak who it's blocked by. And I would several times witness when I was travelling in and out of Sarajevo of UNPROFOR forces in fact using that road and having priority over both my personal traffic, that is government traffic, as well as in fact Bosnian military traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, I would move the admission of pages 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, reference was also made to the first page, and it seems --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Shouldn't we do what we did with the previous exhibits then, and make the whole thing one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. If that works better, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what exhibit number was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, would you make pages 4 and 5 part of Exhibit D24.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, pages 4 and 5 become part of Exhibit D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, could Mr. Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've just been alerted to something, which is page 1, apparently, is not in; it's only page 3. So I think it would be appropriate as well as Ms. Bolton suggested to put page 1 in so that we have the document identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That leaves out only page 2. I'd ask that it be included as well so the whole context of the document is before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. Go ahead. Go ahead, Mr. Registrar. Admit the entire document as Exhibit 24.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The entire document is admitted as Exhibit D24. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to go back for just a brief moment to the answer you just gave, with regard to your assertion that it does not say who it's blocked by. With regard to the sentence "inside the city, UNPROFOR no longer has access to hospitals or to other locations of special interest," you are not contending, are you, that at that time there were Bosnian Serb forces inside of Sarajevo that were blocking access to hospitals? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I am not aware why in fact access was not being given to hospitals, nor am I contending, as you put it, that Bosnian Serbs were blocking, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, that part of Sarajevo was under the control of the Bosnian army, was it not? By that part of Sarajevo I'm referring to that area where there were hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the Bosnian army that I'm referring to is the BiH army, just so we are clear, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to a number of reports, and if you could go to tab 85. I'm sorry, yes, tab 85, which is 65 ter 6615. This is a report of the Secretary-General dated 26 March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like for you to take a look at it, and then I have really but a few questions with regard to this report, and the ensuing reports. Mr. Sacirbey, let me ask you the following as you are reviewing the report, just to interrupt you for a brief second not because I wish to break your train of thought, but rather this report is a report that was produced during a period of time that you were the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is a report, as I understand it, was made for general distribution; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was. I am looking for the key words, but would I suspect it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm looking at the front page --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suspect it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the front page and under distribution it says "general"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a report that you had occasion to read at the time, I'm sure, no?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very honest with you, I was so involved in most of these negotiations that perhaps some of this seems almost second-hand compared to reading it in a report. So I cannot distinguish whether I reviewed it or of course I'm aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the information that's contained within this report, that was distributed generally, you are aware of the information that's contained therein? And I'm not asking you to rush through it. I'm not asking you to rush through it, but that will be my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, you can scroll down, let's see what is written.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I'm trying to review it. It's a little difficult for me to conclude that everything here is something that I have either reviewed or seen in the past. But generally, I'm now, frankly, just scanning it, rather than reviewing it carefully. Yes, it seems to be something I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, when these reports came in and they were distributed generally, one of the things that you did in your capacity as representative for Bosnia-Herzegovina is you reviewed the information that was contained in these reports to make a determination as to whether or not in your view they were accurate or inaccurate, whether they need today be enhanced, or edited, or modified; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either I personally would do that or members of my staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to whether or not you would do it personally, or members of your staff would do it, ultimately the information would be prepared for you. You would be briefed on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I may be. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you may be, is that a possible "may," or are you using the "may" the way you used it previously, as a term of art?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in this instance -- in the instance as it refers to this report, as I said, I was so involved in negotiations, I'm not necessarily familiar with -- let me rephrase that. I just cannot remember if I reviewed this report at the time. As I said, I was so involved in negotiations. Most of the facts here, most of the discussions here seem very familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the best that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have this as Defendant's next in order, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This becomes Exhibit D155. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving to the next tab in the binder which is tab 86, which is -- I'm not going to be able to complete it in the period of time that we have left before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that is convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with the Chamber's indulgence, Mr. Harmon has come down, there is a procedural matter that needs attending to, and I've been asked if I could truncate my examination for a moment so that the matter could be addressed. I don't think it will take terribly long, but it's a matter of some importance with regard to future scheduling. So I would defer at this time to Mr. Lukic and Mr. Harmon, if the Chamber is agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have had a conversation -- first of all, good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, counsel. This afternoon prior to coming into court I was contacted by Mr. Lukic and Mr. Guy-Smith. This morning we produced to the Defence a proofing note, an information report that was the result of a prolonged conversation that we had with the next witness whose name I will not identify at this point because I don't know what protective measures may or may not be imposed, but nevertheless, we were able only to review that proofing note with the witness yesterday. And once it was reviewed and there were corrections made to it, we disclosed it to the Defence. The concern expressed to me by the Defence was it contained a number of new elements that weren't previously -- previously identified in a previous statement. That is correct. I accept that. There's also overlap between what was in the previous statement and what is in this statement. The result of which was the Defence proposed to me that we defer the testimony of this witness until after the break. My proposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: After which break?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After the summer break. After the summer recess. My proposal is as follows, Your Honour: The witness is due to commence his evidence on Thursday. My proposal is that he would start his evidence on Monday. That would permit the Defence a number of extra days to prepare the cross-examination. I would commence my direct examination of the witness on Monday. I anticipate it would take approximately two days, possibly more but not much more than two days if things go as I anticipate. The Defence would then be in a position to cross-examine on the materials that they have received for which -- that is not new because they had information about elements that they've had for a considerable period of time. I've disclosed to the Defence a number of exhibits, potential exhibits. I think at this point it's 55 exhibits. Fifty-one of which are already P exhibits in this case. So there are no surprises in terms of the exhibits themselves. My suggestion would be that the cross-examination then commence. To the extent that the Defence feels it cannot proceed because of the new information and its requirement that it needs additional time, an adjournment can then be sought. And I have checked with the witness, the witness would be in a position to return after the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, without being on either side, would you in your response take into account that the suggestion by Mr. Harmon would possibly enable us to finish with Mr. Sacirbey this week? Just bear that in mind as you configure your argument. I'm sure everybody would like to finish with Mr. Sacirbey at this stage. Not that we don't like you, Mr. Sacirbey, we love to have you here, but still you must be tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply had to wait for the interpretation, and only now I realise the delay takes into the interpretation and actually how much trouble I am for the interpreters. I believe that we can stay in an open session. All of us in the courtroom know which witness we are talking about. This is the gist of the problem. Today at noon we received the additional proofing note of the interview with this witness. This document is 20 pages long in B/C/S and 19 pages in the English version. So it's a rather lengthy document. This is my concern: The proofing notes concerning this interview have to do with an interview that Mr. Harmon made with this witness during the four last days of April of this year, so on the 27th, 28th, 29th, and 30th of April. And the proofing note was compiled on the 1st of May. This is what it stated here. I can see here that the witness signed this note in the language that he understands yesterday. However, we only received this very significant proofing note concerning this very significant witness today, and I believe that we simply did not have time enough to get prepared, because this is a very significant witness. The testimony that will go into the very core of this -- this particular case. And I would really not like to have to interrupt my cross-examination of this witness because I will simply not be able to start with one concept of cross-examination and then to have to change. And given that I received this material only today at noon, I do not believe that I will be capable of getting prepared by Monday of next week. So this is a very fundamental issue that has to do with Article 21 of the statute. And I will tell you very briefly what my proposal would be. Given that this is one of the key witnesses of this particular trial, also in light of the fact that there is a great number of new facts that the witness will testify on, I agree with Mr. Harmon that the documents that were available to us, but it is not the documents that are problematic here, but rather the attitude of this witness towards these documents as results from the proofing note. My proposal would be either not to start with this witness giving testimony here before the end of the summer recess, or for Mr. Harmon to have his examination-in-chief next week and then for my cross-examination to start after the summer break. Because these few days are simply insufficient for me to make all the checks that I believe I need to make to prepare for my cross-examination. So really it's been two and a half months since the interview with this witness, and I only received the proofing note today, so I believe that this is in contravention of Article 21, and it simply doesn't allow me enough space.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have told us that the witness only signed yesterday. They couldn't give you a proofing note that is not signed, I would imagine. What made it be signed only yesterday and not when it was drafted, that's another matter we don't know. Now, if I may suggest, Mr. Harmon, you said you would need two to three days to lead your evidence in chief with this witness. That would mean if we accommodate Mr. Lukic and not -- and he does not start with his cross-examination, we would lose three days of next week. Given what he is saying, is that fatal? I mean, can't we accommodate him? You lead your witness next week and take your time. If you take three days, it's three days, and then we break off and then he starts his cross-examination after the recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Of course it's not fatal, Your Honour. I was thinking in terms of judicial economy in the sense that there are a large number of subjects about which this witness would testify. In my respectful submission, the cross-examination could commence on those subjects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I understand that. But, you know, Mr. Lukic has said what he has said about starting cross-examination next week, it's not about the document; it's about the attitude of the witness. Whatever the attitude is, I don't know. And he is raising a more important point which when balanced against judicial economy, it seems to weigh heavier, namely the rights of the accused, at least in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am at your disposal on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can we quickly then agree that the Prosecution will lead evidence, and then you [indiscernible] on this witness, and we'll break off and the cross-examination will start in the new term. Okay. So be it ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one request, however, in respect of the Court's now -- its decision. May the testimony of the witness commence on Monday the 24th of August for the following reason: I will be not available on the first day of the return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are getting a larger slice of the recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am getting a larger slice of the recess by one day. And I will not be available, I'll be in transit back to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We recess -- we are supposed to start on the 17th of August, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. 17th would be fine then, Your Honour. I am sorry. Let me check with Mr. Thomas. I believe we have a witness who is scheduled on the 17th and the 18th. We have potential witnesses for the remaining --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Days of that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- days of that week. We are still working on the scheduling of those witnesses, but we have allotted some time to those witnesses so that following week would be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And you say you are available from the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am available for the 24th for the testimony of that witness. I am available earlier, but I believe there is -- if I can have just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in consultation with Mr. Thomas, it appears that the witnesses starting on the 19th are not firmly scheduled, so we could start with this witness on the 19th, if the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you be back?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will be back, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We will not say anything about when he will start at this point. We will hear from you. If it's the 19th, it will be the 19th. If you schedule other witnesses 19th, 20, 21st, you will do so, and you can start on the 24th. But all we'll say for now is that we agree that his cross-examination begins after recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you very much. May I be excused, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Sacirbey, sorry for that. We had to do this also in the interest of getting you finished with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before my learned friend begins, I didn't want to interrupt our proceedings. At about half an hour or so, I will be needed elsewhere. I will be replaced in the courtroom by Mr. Saxon. I was wondering if I could just be excused at that point without further reference to Your Honours, and for Mr. Saxon to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You just want to sneak out, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could have 6090 up on the screen. That would be tab 86 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I believe you have tab 85. I'm -- sorry, you have tab 86. It's coming up on the screen. This document is once again a document that was distributed generally; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to the second page of the document. This document is dated -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, 1D03. I do apologise, Mr. Registrar. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it 1D03 before the 6090?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 25th of June, 1995. And it's a report by the co-chairman of the steering committee of the international conference on the former Yugoslavia. And I'd like to go to the second page of the document, page 2, paragraph number 3. And with regard to the language contained therein, it's the very last sentence on this page, which is: "The co-chairmen also conclude that during the period covered by the present report there have been no commercial trans-shipments across the border between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving to page 4 of this report, paragraph 10 indicates: "The Mission continues to enjoy full freedom of movement within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving to paragraph 16 on page 5, with regard to the cooperation from the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, they continue to be good; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thereafter at paragraph 19, there is a discussion about smuggling of fuel and the interdiction of such smuggling effort -- of such smuggling; correct? It goes on from --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: 19, 20, 21, 22, and there's a continuing discussion with regard to customs officials interdicting black-market officials; right?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it this is a document that you received in your capacity as ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have this marked as --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] As foreign minister at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can I have this marked as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This becomes Exhibit D156. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next tab in your binder, sir, which is tab number 87, which would be 1D03-6082.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a letter dated 19 September, 1994, the distribution is once again, as I understand it, general. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If I could refer to you page 3 specifically. In which the report states: "Closure by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of its border with the Bosnian Serbs..."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This indicates that on the 4th of August, the following measures were ordered by the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to come in effect the same day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And it lists three specific measures that are to come into effect; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To break off political and economic relations with Republika Srpska, to prohibit the stay of members of the leadership of Republika Srpska in the territory of FRY, and as of today the border of the FRY is closed for all transport towards Republika Srpska except food, clothing, and medicine; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could turn to page 6 of the same document, sir. With regard to the Mission concept, and looking -- directing your attention to paragraph 19 with regard to the Mission concept, there's an indication: "The Mission will exercise its right to go wherever it wishes without any form of prior notification to follow the work of customs officers of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) and to actually look into vehicles crossing the border." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is a document, this is actually a letter that you also received in your capacity as ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have that marked as Defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit D157. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next tab in your binder, that would be tab number 88, which is 1D03-6050.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again this is a general distribution; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And this is the discussion of UNPROFOR; true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It seems at least in part. I haven't reviewed the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you'd like to take a moment to look at it, that will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at least that seems to be the lion's share of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn to paragraph 30, if you could, which is on page 10 of the hard copy, and I'll tell --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the issue of safe areas, if you go about halfway in the paragraph, this was something that we had been discussing, I believe, the other day, which specific day, to be perfectly honest with you, Mr. Sacirbey, I don't remember, but we discussed the issue of the use of safe areas.
